tactics.name: Reconnaissance
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to gather information they can use to plan future operations.

tactics.name: Resource Development
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to establish resources they can use to support operations.

tactics.name: Initial Access
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to get into your network.

tactics.name: Execution
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to run malicious code.

tactics.name: Persistence
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to maintain their foothold.

tactics.name: Privilege Escalation
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to gain higher-level permissions.

tactics.name: Defense Evasion
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to avoid being detected.

tactics.name: Credential Access
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to steal account names and passwords.

tactics.name: Discovery
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to figure out your environment.

tactics.name: Lateral Movement
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to move through your environment.

tactics.name: Collection
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to gather data of interest to their goal.

tactics.name: Command and Control
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to communicate with compromised systems to control them.

tactics.name: Exfiltration
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to steal data.

tactics.name: Impact
tactics.description: The adversary is trying to manipulate, interrupt, or destroy your systems and data.

techniques.name: Phishing
techniques.description: Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems.
techniques.detection: Network intrusion detection systems and email gateways can be used to detect phishing.

techniques.name: Spearphishing Attachment
techniques.description: Adversaries may send spearphishing emails with a malicious attachment in an attempt to gain access.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries.

techniques.name: PowerShell
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution.

techniques.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
techniques.description: Adversaries may configure system settings to automatically execute a program during system boot or logon.

techniques.name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
techniques.description: Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a program to a startup folder or referencing it with a Registry run key.

techniques.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents.

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material.

techniques.name: LSASS Memory
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the LSASS.

techniques.name: System Information Discovery
techniques.description: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware.

techniques.name: Remote Services
techniques.description: Adversaries may use valid accounts to log into a service specifically designed to accept remote connections.

techniques.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol.

techniques.name: Application Layer Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols to avoid detection.

techniques.name: Web Protocols
techniques.description: Adversaries may communicate using application layer protocols associated with web traffic.

techniques.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel.

techniques.name: Data Encrypted for Impact
techniques.description: Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems or on large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability.

techniques.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to take advantage of a weakness in an Internet-facing computer or program using software, data, or commands.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts
techniques.description: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

techniques.name: Process Injection
techniques.description: Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

techniques.name: Scheduled Task/Job
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

techniques.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
techniques.description: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files from an external system into a compromised environment.

techniques.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
techniques.description: Adversaries may use obfuscated files or information to hide artifacts of an intrusion from analysis.

techniques.name: User Execution
techniques.description: An adversary may rely upon specific actions by a user in order to gain execution.

techniques.name: Masquerading
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and security tools.

techniques.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
techniques.description: Adversaries may use a non-application layer protocol for communication between host and C2 server.

techniques.name: Impair Defenses
techniques.description: Adversaries may maliciously modify components of a victim environment in order to hinder or disable defensive mechanisms.

techniques.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
techniques.description: Adversaries may abuse WMI to execute malicious commands and payloads.

techniques.name: Archive Collected Data
techniques.description: An adversary may compress and/or encrypt data that is collected prior to exfiltration.

techniques.name: Gather Victim Host Information
techniques.description: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's hosts that can be used during targeting.

techniques.name: Acquire Infrastructure
techniques.description: Adversaries may buy, lease, or rent infrastructure that can be used during targeting.

groups.name: APT28
groups.description: APT28 is a threat group that has been attributed to Russia's General Staff Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU) 85th Main Special Service Center (GTsSS) military unit 26165.

groups.name: APT29
groups.description: APT29 is a threat group that has been attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). They have operated since at least 2008.

groups.name: Lazarus Group
groups.description: Lazarus Group is a North Korean state-sponsored cyber threat group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau.

groups.name: APT41
groups.description: APT41 is a threat group that carries out Chinese state-sponsored espionage activity in addition to financially motivated activity.

groups.name: Turla
groups.description: Turla is a Russian-based threat group that has infected victims in over 45 countries, spanning a range of industries including government, embassies, military, education, research and pharmaceutical companies since 2004.

groups.name: Sandworm Team
groups.description: Sandworm Team is a destructive threat group attributed to Russia's GRU Main Center for Special Technologies (GTsST) military unit 74455.

groups.name: Magic Hound
groups.description: Magic Hound is an Iranian-sponsored threat group that has conducted espionage campaigns targeting energy, government, and technology sectors in Europe and North America.

groups.name: Kimsuky
groups.description: Kimsuky is a North Korea-based cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012, primarily targeting South Korean think tanks and government entities.

groups.name: APT32
groups.description: APT32 is a suspected Vietnam-based threat group that has been active since at least 2014 targeting foreign corporations with a vested interest in Vietnam's manufacturing, consumer products, and hospitality sectors.

groups.name: Threat Group-3390
groups.description: Threat Group-3390 is a Chinese threat group that has extensively used strategic web compromises to target victims. The group has been active since at least 2010.

groups.name: Dragonfly
groups.description: Dragonfly is a cyber espionage group that has been attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). Active since at least 2010, primarily targeting the energy sector.

groups.name: menuPass
groups.description: menuPass is a threat group that has been active since at least 2006, attributed to Chinese Ministry of State Security's (MSS) Tianjin State Security Bureau.

software.name: Cobalt Strike
software.description: Cobalt Strike is a commercial, full-featured, remote access tool that bills itself as adversary simulation software.

software.name: Mimikatz
software.description: Mimikatz is a credential dumper capable of obtaining plaintext Windows account logins and passwords.

software.name: Duqu
software.description: Duqu is a malware platform that appears to be closely related to the Stuxnet worm.

software.name: KeyBoy
software.description: KeyBoy is a custom malware used by threat groups for data collection and exfiltration.

software.name: njRAT
software.description: njRAT is a remote access trojan first observed in 2012, commonly used by threat actors in the Middle East.

software.name: Uroburos
software.description: Uroburos is a rootkit used by Turla. It intercepts network traffic and can exfiltrate data.

software.name: NotPetya
software.description: NotPetya is malware that was used by Sandworm Team in a worldwide attack starting on June 27, 2017.

software.name: Astaroth
software.description: Astaroth is a Trojan and information stealer known to affect companies in Europe and Brazil.

software.name: Net Crawler
software.description: Net Crawler is a network-propagating worm used by threat actors to move laterally within compromised networks.

software.name: InvisiMole
software.description: InvisiMole is a modular spyware that has been used by threat groups since at least 2013, targeting a small number of high-profile victims.

software.name: TrickBot
software.description: TrickBot is a Trojan/botnet that primarily targets financial institutions, later expanded to deliver ransomware.

software.name: Emotet
software.description: Emotet is a modular malware variant which is primarily used as a downloader for other malware variants.

software.name: IcedID
software.description: IcedID is a modular banking trojan first discovered in 2017, used by multiple groups to deliver additional payloads.

software.name: QakBot
software.description: QakBot is a modular banking trojan active since 2007, commonly distributed through phishing emails with malicious attachments.

software.name: PsExec
software.description: PsExec is a free Microsoft tool that can be used to execute a process on another computer.
